questions.prompt: In C++26, what does this program print?
options: Nothing: a structured binding pack must be the last name in the list
questions.explanation: `first` binds to `x`, and the structured binding pack `rest` takes the remaining two members, so `sizeof...(rest)` is 2 and the result is `1 * 100 + 2`. `103` comes from counting every binding rather than only the pack's elements. A pack may appear anywhere in the list, not only at the end, and this declaration is inside a function template, as P1061R10 requires.

questions.prompt: In C++26, for the call `f(1, 'c')`, what type is `R`?
options: `int&`, because `xs...[0]` is an lvalue
`int`
`int&&`
Ill-formed: `decltype` cannot be applied to a pack-index-expression
questions.explanation: A pack-index-expression is an id-expression, and its instantiation is simply the name of the selected parameter. `decltype` of an unparenthesized id-expression is the declared type of the entity, which is `int`. The `int&` answer is what `decltype((xs...[0]))` gives, because the extra parentheses make `decltype` look at the value category, which is lvalue.

questions.prompt: In C++26, which member declaration is ill-formed?
options: None of them
questions.explanation: P2893R3 lets a friend-type-declaration take a list of friend-type-specifiers, each of which may be a pack expansion, so `#1` and `#2` are valid C++26. `#3` uses an elaborated-type-specifier, and [dcl.type.elab] makes `class` followed by a name that resolves to a template parameter ill-formed. That rule already rejected `friend class T;` before C++26. Write `friend Ts...;` instead.

questions.prompt: In C++26, what happens with this call?
questions.code:
template<class... T> void first(T...[0] x) {}

int main() { first(1); }
options: `T` is deduced as `{int}` and `first<int>` is called
Ill-formed: no matching function, because `T` cannot be deduced from a pack-index-specifier
Undefined behavior: the index is out of range at run time
Ill-formed: a pack-index-specifier cannot be used as a parameter type
questions.explanation: A pack-index-specifier is a non-deduced context, so the argument `1` contributes nothing to deducing `T`. The trailing pack `T` is therefore deduced as empty, and substituting it makes `T...[0]` an out-of-range index, so the only candidate fails and the call has no match. Indexing cannot be undefined behavior, because the index is a constant checked at compile time. `first<int>(1)` works.

questions.prompt: In C++26, what is the type of `pick<2, 0>(1, 'c', 3.0)`?
options: `std::tuple<double, int>`
`std::tuple<int, char, double>`
`std::tuple<char, int>`
Ill-formed: `I` and `T` are expanded by the same ellipsis but have different lengths
questions.explanation: In `T...[I]...` the first ellipsis is part of the pack-index-specifier, and that construct's pattern only expands `T` in place. The outer ellipsis is an ordinary pack expansion whose only unexpanded pack is `I`, so it produces `T...[2], T...[0]`, which is `double, int`. The length-mismatch answer would be right if both packs were expanded by the outer ellipsis, but `T` is consumed by the indexing.

questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft, is this function well-formed?
options: Well-formed, and it returns 6
Well-formed only if `f` is declared `constexpr`
Ill-formed: a structured binding pack can only be introduced in a templated entity
Ill-formed: a structured binding pack cannot follow a named binding
questions.explanation: [dcl.pre] requires a structured binding declaration that contains a pack to declare a templated entity, and `f` is an ordinary function. An earlier revision, P1061R9, allowed this by creating an implicit template region, but that design was rejected, and R10 restricted packs to templates. Wrapping the same code in a template or a generic lambda makes it valid and returns 6.

questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft, with P2963 applied, what does `k(1, 2)` do?
options: Calls `#2`, because "all are integral" implies "some is integral"
Calls `#1`, because a disjunction is satisfied first
Ill-formed: fold expressions are not allowed in a requires-clause
The call is ambiguous
questions.explanation: Both folds normalize to fold expanded constraints, and [temp.constr.order] lets one subsume the other only if they have the same fold-operator. Here the operators differ, so neither declaration is more constrained and the call is ambiguous. The implication answer fails on empty packs: `(C<T> && ...)` is satisfied for an empty pack and `(C<T> || ...)` is not, which is exactly why P2963 requires matching operators. Clang 21 reports the ambiguity. GCC 16 also does, but only because it does not implement P2963 at all.

questions.prompt: Under the C++26 draft (P2841R7), which template argument is valid for `V`?
options: `zero`, as in `at_int<zero>`
`zero<int>`, as in `at_int<zero<int>>`
`Small`, because a concept is a kind of variable template of type `bool`
`Box`, because any template whose parameter list matches is accepted
questions.explanation: `template<class> auto V` is a variable template template parameter, and [temp.arg.template] says its argument must name a variable template or another variable template template parameter. `zero` is a variable template. `zero<int>` is a value, not a template. A concept is not a variable template, and it needs a concept template parameter of the form `template<class> concept C`. A class template needs a type template template parameter. No compiler available here implements P2841 yet, so this answer rests on the draft text.
